sharedText: it came to pass that after the
reason: A seven-word run and the top-ranked candidate at this verse, and every word of it is the Book of Mormon's standing narrative hinge. 1 Chronicles 20:1 dates the siege of Rabbah; Mormon 8:2 dates the hunting down of the Nephite remnant after Cumorah. The machine ranked it because 'that after the' happens to be rare after 'it came to pass', which is an accident of the KJV's own connective habits, not a signal. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

Genuinely tempting, and it is recorded as composite on the accepted link rather than discarded. Job 19:14 — 'My kinsfolk have failed, and my familiar friends have forgotten me' — is one of only two KJV verses containing both words, and Job's register of total desolation is Moroni's register here. It loses to Luke 21:16 on two grounds: 1830 spells the word 'kinsfolks', which is Luke's spelling and not Job's (1920 normalised it to Job's, which is why the current text points the other way), and Luke 21:16 is the only one of the two in which the kinsfolk are put to death. See the link at 8:5.

Five words of pure connective tissue. Numbers 35:32 legislates the manslayer's confinement to a city of refuge until the high priest dies; Mormon 8:10 says the three disciples tarried in the land until the wickedness became too great. The shared string is a preposition, an article, a noun the Book of Mormon uses on nearly every page, and a temporal conjunction. This entry also covers Judges 1:34 at the same verse ('would not suffer them to', of the Amorites forcing the Danites into the mountain), which is the same kind of match on a modal construction.

'Make an end of' is the King James Bible's ordinary phrase for finishing or destroying and it occurs across Genesis, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Daniel. Ezekiel 20:17 is a verse about the LORD sparing Israel in the wilderness rather than making an end of them, i.e. the destructive sense; Moroni is closing a section of a book, the compositional sense. The Book of Mormon uses the compositional sense constantly — Nephi, Jacob, Mormon and Moroni all 'make an end' of speaking or writing — so no single KJV verse can be behind it.

The obvious candidate for 'it shall be brought out of darkness unto light … and it shall shine forth out of darkness', and it will not carry. 'out of darkness' occurs in exactly seven KJV verses, spread over Job, Psalms, Isaiah, 2 Corinthians and 1 Peter, so the phrase points nowhere in particular; and the one thing that would make 1 Peter 2:9 identifiable — 'into his marvellous light' — is precisely what Moroni does not have, though he uses 'marvellous' twice elsewhere in the chapter. Recorded because a reader who knows 1 Peter will expect to find it here and should be told it was considered. The link actually made at this verse is to 1 Timothy 2:4.

The machine's top candidate at this verse and a straightforward misfire. Haggai 2:8 is 'The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, saith the LORD of hosts', a promise about temple funding; the five shared words are a possessive plus the KJV's commonest prophetic tag. Moroni's verse is a signed quotation of Romans 12:19, which has the identical tag for the identical reason — Paul supplied 'saith the Lord' when he quoted Deuteronomy 32:35, which does not have it. Superseded by the link at 8:20.

Five words spanning a clause boundary, four of them structural. Exodus 3:13 is Moses asking God for a name to give the children of Israel; Mormon 8:21 is a description of men who deny that God will remember his covenant with the house of Israel. 'The house of Israel' is one of the Book of Mormon's most frequent phrases and 'and shall say' introduces speech everywhere in both books. Nothing survives contact.

'As the LORD liveth' occurs in exactly twenty-seven KJV verses and is the King James oath formula; that the next word happens to be 'he' in both places is arithmetic. 1 Samuel 19:6 is Saul swearing to Jonathan that David shall not be slain. The Book of Mormon uses the formula throughout and it carries no intertextual signal here.

Worth recording because the temptation is real and the evidence is one word. 'Search the scriptures' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the King James Bible's only imperative of its kind; Moroni writes 'Search the prophecies of Isaiah', which is the same imperative with a different object. The metalepsis would be attractive — John 5:39 continues 'they are they which testify of me' — but the contact is a single common verb plus a genre noun that differs, and an accepted link on that basis would license a hundred more. The Isaiah 29 material this verse actually depends on is adjudicated in the link at 8:23, and it reaches Moroni through 2 Nephi rather than through the KJV.

sharedText: shall cry unto the LORD because of the
reason: The strongest displaced candidate in the chapter, with an eight-word contiguous run and a matching sense — Isaiah 19:20's Egyptians 'shall cry unto the LORD because of the oppressors, and he shall send them a saviour'. It is displaced rather than refuted. What makes Moroni's clause identifiable is not the crying, which is common ('cry unto the LORD' occurs in exactly seven KJV verses), but the subject of it: the blood of saints. 'blood of saints' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 16:6, and 'avenge our blood' in exactly one, Revelation 6:10 — the verse Moroni returns to at 8:41. Isaiah's criers are living men under a foreign yoke; Moroni's are the dead. See the link at 8:27.

'Transfigured' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 17:2 and Mark 9:2, and both are the Transfiguration; there is no other use of the word in the King James Bible. Moroni's 'Why have ye transfigured the holy word of God?' is therefore a striking collocation and it is not a borrowing. In the gospels the word names a glorification — a face shining as the sun, raiment white as the light — and it is done to Christ by God; in Moroni it names a corruption, done to scripture by men, and the nearest biblical idea is 2 Corinthians 2:17's 'which corrupt the word of God', which shares no vocabulary with it at all. The word is doing the opposite work in the two texts, which is the definition of this category.

A real contact with the right discourse and the wrong evangelist. Luke 21:7 is the disciples' question that opens Luke's Olivet Discourse, and this chapter is demonstrably built on that discourse — but on Matthew's version of it, not Luke's: the anaphora at 8:26-32 is Matthew 24:50's 'shall come in a day when' rather than Luke 12:46's 'will come', the signs at 8:30 are Matthew 24:6-7's, and the 'hypocrites' Moroni names at 8:38 are the portion assigned in Matthew 24:51 and not in Luke 12:46. The five shared words here are the interrogative frame both evangelists use. Superseded by the links at 8:26 and 8:30.

'The pride of their hearts' is a Book of Mormon signature and occurs in exactly zero KJV verses; what the machine matched is the generic 'because of the pride of', which Job 35:12 completes with 'evil men' in a verse about unanswered prayer. The Book of Mormon runs this phrase from Jacob to Moroni — pride of their hearts, pride of your hearts, lifted up in the pride — as its standing diagnosis of prosperity, and no KJV verse is behind it. This entry covers the same match wherever it recurs in Mormon.

A case where a singleton count is arithmetic rather than evidence, and worth spelling out because the count looks decisive. 'the poor and the needy', with both articles, occurs in exactly one KJV verse — but 'poor and needy' without them is one of the commonest social formulas in the Bible, at Deuteronomy 24:14, Psalm 72:13, Psalm 82:4, Proverbs 31:9, Ezekiel 16:49, 18:12, 22:29 and Amos 4:1 among others. Psalm 35:10 is a thanksgiving for personal deliverance from a strong enemy; Mormon 8:37 is an indictment of churches that love money more than the poor. The real dependence in these verses is on James 5:1-4 and is adjudicated at 8:38. This entry covers 'the sick and the afflicted' in the same verse for the same reason.

1 Peter 3:3 — 'that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel' — is the New Testament's set piece against ornament, and Moroni's 'Why do ye adorn yourselves with that which hath no life' sits four words from 'the adorning of your churches' in the previous verse. It is still one shared root. Peter is addressing wives about their own dress and contrasting it with a meek and quiet spirit; Moroni is addressing church leaders about gilding buildings while the poor go past, and the phrase he uses of the ornaments — 'that which hath no life' — has no biblical parallel and is the sharpest thing in the sentence. The link recorded in this stretch is to James 5:3 at 8:38, whose subject is the same money.
